summary: Defines how to use the Diffie-Hellman algorithms X25519 and X448 and the signature algorithms Ed25519 and Ed448 in JOSE, the JSON-based signing and encryption framework.

eli5.summary: JSON web tokens need locks and stamps. This tells them how to use some newer, well-liked kinds of locks and stamps.

subtitle: How JOSE carries the modern X25519, X448, Ed25519 and Ed448 algorithms: one new key type and one new signature name.

tldr.problem: The IRTF CFRG selected new Diffie-Hellman and signature algorithms, but JOSE had no agreed way to carry their keys or signatures in JSON.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new key type, OKP (Octet Key Pair), the signature algorithm name EdDSA, and the curve names Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448, and says how to apply them to JWS signing and ECDH-ES key agreement.
tldr.outcome: JOSE implementations can use these algorithms interoperably. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9864.

today: RFC 8037 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9864, so read the two together. The OKP key type and the EdDSA, Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448 names it registered are the ones it defines.

sections.title: Why JOSE Needs These Algorithms
sections.content:
The IRTF Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) selected new Diffie-Hellman algorithms (X25519 and X448, from RFC 7748) and signature algorithms (Ed25519 and Ed448, from RFC 8032). This document defines how to use them in JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) in an interoperable manner.

The conventions apply in the context of JWS (RFC 7515), JWE (RFC 7516) and JWK (RFC 7517).

The CFRG also defined two pairs of isogenous elliptic curves under these algorithms. The RFC does not expose those curves directly, because the algorithms on top are enough for JOSE and are much easier to use. All inputs and outputs of the ECDH and signature functions are octet strings, except the result of verification, which is a boolean.
sections.eli5: There are some new, popular kinds of secret codes. This RFC teaches the JSON toolbox how to use them, without making people learn the tricky maths underneath.

sections.title: The OKP Key Type
sections.content:
A new key type (kty) value, OKP (Octet Key Pair), is defined for public key algorithms that use octet strings as private and public keys. It has these parameters:

  • kty MUST be OKP.
  • crv MUST be present and holds the subtype of the key, from the JSON Web Elliptic Curve registry.
  • x MUST be present and holds the public key, base64url encoded.
  • d MUST be present for private keys, base64url encoded, and MUST NOT be present for public keys.

The RFC adds a warning: do not assume there is an underlying elliptic curve just because the parameters are named crv and x. The key type could be extended to other Diffie-Hellman algorithms, for example ones based on hyperelliptic surfaces.

When computing a JWK Thumbprint (RFC 7638), the three public key fields go into the hash input in lexicographic order: crv, kty, x.
sections.eli5: An OKP key is a label on a box of bytes saying what kind of key it is. The public part goes in one slot and the secret part, if there is one, in another.

sections.title: Signing with EdDSA
sections.content:
For signing with JWS, the algorithm name EdDSA is defined as a value of the alg parameter. The key subtypes (crv values) for it are Ed25519 and Ed448, always with key type OKP. The EdDSA variant used is determined by the key's subtype. These subtypes MUST NOT be used for ECDH-ES.

Signing applies the signing algorithm of RFC 8032 to the private key, the public key and the JWS Signing Input (as the message). The result is the JWS Signature.

Verification applies the RFC 8032 verification algorithm to the public key, the JWS Signing Input and the JWS Signature. If the algorithm accepts, the signature is valid; otherwise it is invalid.
sections.eli5: To sign, you stamp the message with your secret key. To check, anyone uses your public key to see whether the stamp is real.

sections.title: Key Agreement with ECDH-ES
sections.content:
For Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Static (ECDH-ES) key agreement, the key subtypes X25519 and X448 are defined, again with key type OKP. They MUST NOT be used for signing. The ECDH-ES algorithms themselves (ECDH-ES, ECDH-ES+A128KW, ECDH-ES+A192KW and ECDH-ES+A256KW) come from Section 4.6 of RFC 7518.

To build the sender's ephemeral public key, apply the ECDH function to the ephemeral private key (scalar input) and the standard base point (u-coordinate input). The base64url encoding of the output becomes the x parameter of the epk field.

The shared value Z comes from applying the ECDH function to the ephemeral private key (scalar input) and the receiver's public key (u-coordinate input). Z then goes into the key derivation function from RFC 7518.
sections.eli5: Two people each mix their own secret with the other's public number and end up with the same shared secret, without ever sending it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7748 and RFC 8032 apply. Beyond that, the RFC gives these warnings:

  • Keep key material together with the information about what key subtype it is for, and check that the algorithm is compatible with the key. Mixing up algorithms opens the system to attacks, and mixing up signature and MAC algorithms is particularly dangerous.
  • Ed25519 and Ed448 signatures bind the signing key, but do not assume this. If key binding is wanted, include the key in the JWS protected header or in the data to sign.
  • Key generation and batch signature verification REQUIRE a well-seeded cryptographic random number generator. Signing and non-batch verification are deterministic and need no random numbers.
  • The JWA ECDH-ES KDF construction does not mix keys into the final shared secret. Problems need a malicious receiver key or a malicious sender, but in either case all security evaporates.
  • The nominal security strengths of X25519 and X448 are about 126 and 223 bits, so using 256-bit symmetric encryption with X448 is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Do not mix up your keys: a key for stamping must never be used for secret-sharing, and the other way round. Keep a label on every key.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC adds entries to several JOSE registries, all with the IESG as change controller and with JOSE implementation requirement Optional.

  • JSON Web Key Types: OKP, described as octet string key pairs.
  • JSON Web Key Parameters: crv (the subtype of key pair), d (the private key) and x (the public key), all used with OKP.
  • JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms: EdDSA.
  • JSON Web Key Elliptic Curve: Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448.

Appendix A gives worked examples, mostly taken from the test vectors of RFC 7748 and RFC 8032: an Ed25519 key, its JWK thumbprint, a signed JWS, and ECDH-ES exchanges with X25519 and X448.
sections.eli5: The new names were written into the official list of names so nobody else uses them for something different.
